analysis.one_liner: Makes households with over $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets pay tax on investment gains every year.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 17, 2025 with 34 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the ultra-wealthy to pay income tax on their investment gains every year, the same way workers pay tax on wages, instead of being able to put off tax indefinitely. It targets strategies like 'buy, borrow, die' — buying assets that grow in value, borrowing against them to fund living costs, and passing them to heirs untaxed. It applies only to people with more than $100 million in yearly income or more than $1 billion in assets, and it also closes more than 30 related loopholes covering trusts, compensation, and business swaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit from a rule that treats the largest fortunes the way wages are treated: taxed annually rather than deferred until death. Because gains on unsold stock and businesses would be counted each year, the deferral games that let a small number of families accumulate untaxed wealth would end. Any revenue raised is unspecified in the bill, so the direct benefit to working households is mainly fairness and whatever Congress later chooses to do with the money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers, under current deferral rules

how_it_helps.text: Requires taxpayers with over $100 million in adjusted gross income or over $1 billion in covered assets (for three straight years) to recognize gains and losses annually, as if unsold tradable assets were sold at fair market value at year end.
Treats gifts, bequests, and transfers in trust of covered assets as a sale at fair market value, ending the stepped-up basis rule that lets heirs sell inherited assets tax-free.

Closes deferral routes beyond stocks: it reaches swaps, like-kind real estate exchanges, transfers in exchange for stock, deferred compensation, certain life insurance and annuity contracts, and holdings in partnerships and other pass-through entities, with special reporting and anti-avoidance rules to keep the ultra-wealthy from restructuring around it.

Eases the transition: a newly covered taxpayer can pay the first year's extra mark-to-market tax in five annual installments, and the deferral recapture charge on nontradable assets is capped and only applied when the asset is actually transferred.

analysis.who_pays: A very small number of ultra-wealthy households — those with more than $100 million of yearly income or $1 billion in assets — plus the estate planners, private fund managers, and tax advisors whose business depends on the deferral strategies the bill shuts down. Retirement accounts, IRAs, 529s, HSAs, and cash are excluded from the tax.

drawbacks.text: Taxing gains on assets that have not been sold creates annual valuation problems, especially for private businesses and other nontradable assets; the bill handles this with multiple valuation methods (original cost, adjusted basis, appraisals, financial statements, loan values) and leaves many details to Treasury regulations.

Tax can come due on paper gains before any cash is realized; the bill softens this with a first-year five-year installment election, loss carrybacks, and a cap on the deferral recapture charge, but the administration burden for covered families and their business entities is large.

The bill anticipates avoidance and exit: it applies to expatriates for ten years after they give up citizenship and subjects them to lower thresholds, which signals the drafters' concern that covered taxpayers would renounce citizenship or move assets offshore rather than pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — taxing the largest fortunes annually instead of letting gains compound tax-free until death — directly addresses a genuine gap between how wages and wealth are taxed. The costs are real but narrow: significant valuation and compliance complexity concentrated on a few thousand households, and unresolved legal challenges over taxing unrealized gains would be likely. Nothing in the bill directs new revenue to any specific benefit for working people, so its concrete upside for them depends on later spending decisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where the chair has taken no action on it, so it sits with no scheduled hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act in the House on September 17, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.
Thirty-three House Democrats joined Cohen as cosponsors; no Republicans are listed.
The bill would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, so it has no effect until enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ultra-wealthy households are better off so far, because the bill has gone nowhere and the current rules that let investment gains go untaxed for decades remain in place. So do the tax planners and estate advisors whose services depend on those rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ultra-wealthy households and their tax planners

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 33 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican majority controls the Ways and Means Committee calendar where the bill now sits.

industries.note: The bill ends the ability to hold appreciated assets, borrow against them tax-free, and pass them to heirs without tax — the core benefit wealthy families currently get from deferral. Their interest in keeping that benefit runs directly against the public interest in a tax system that taxes gains annually.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge funds, and pass-through business owners
industries.note: The bill reaches ownership interests in partnerships and other pass-through entities, requires entity reporting to covered owners, and eliminates deferral on certain compensation. Fund managers and large private-business owners would owe tax on gains annually instead of when they choose to sell.

industries.industry: Estate planning and tax advisory firms
industries.note: Strategies the bill targets — 'buy, borrow, die', grantor trust planning, private placement life insurance — are a large fee business built on deferral. Closing the loopholes shrinks the market for that advice, though some demand shifts to compliance work under the new mark-to-market rules.

industries.industry: Private placement life insurance and annuity providers
industries.note: These contracts are currently a favored vehicle for holding investments outside the income tax; the bill counts their cash surrender value toward the asset threshold and directs the Treasury to write rules ensuring the value reflects underlying investments so the vehicle cannot be used to avoid the tax.

Like-kind (1031) exchanges would no longer indefinitely defer gain for covered taxpayers, and investments in qualified opportunity funds would be treated as nontradable assets. The effect falls only on the biggest, wealthiest holders, not ordinary property owners.

analysis.trajectory: With 34 Democratic sponsors, no Republican support, and a Ways and Means Committee chaired by a Republican who has taken no action, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress. Comparable billionaire-tax proposals in recent Congresses have died in committee the same way. Its realistic path is as a marker for future Democratic tax packages rather than a law in this session.
